newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tax rise casts cloud over Japan economic recovery.
newsitem.headline: Tax rise casts cloud over Japan economic recovery.

text.p: A set of statistics this week has shown that higher taxes are taking a toll on the Japanese economy, but officials say the impact is temporary and insist the country has not fallen off its recovery track.

A surprising drop in industrial production figures jolted markets on Thursday, and the bad news was followed on Friday by bleak jobless statistics and more data showing a fall in housing construction.
The latest figures have made an interest rate rise seem a more distant prospect than it appeared earlier in the week.

Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, commenting on Friday on last month's fall in industrial production, said the effects of a rise in the national sales tax in April will be felt in the April-June quarter but they should start to wear off in the next quarter.

Earlier this week, Bank of Japan (BOJ) Governor Yasuo Matsushita said that the negative effects of the tax increase were being felt most strongly at present, but that the economy's recovery trend was intact. The sales tax was raised to five percent from three percent on April 1.

On Thursday, financial markets were jolted by the unexpectedly poor output data showing that industrial production dropped 0.4 percent in April from the previous month on a seasonally adjusted basis, hit by the tax rise and subsequently weak orders.
This dampened market expectations of an early interest rate rise, triggering a fall in Japanese government bond yields and a sell-off of the yen.

Earlier in the week, speculation of an imminent rise in the official discount rate was fuelled when the BOJ announced that its closely watched quarterly "tankan" survey of corporate sentiment survey would be released in June rather than July.

On Friday, the government announced Japan's housing starts fell 9.3 percent in April from a year earlier to 126,318 units, dropping for the fourth consecutive month on a year-on-year basis. Private home construction was particularly hard hit, with starts dropping 27.8 percent from the previous year.
The Construction Ministry cited the tax increase dampening demand for new houses, saying overall housing starts will continue to decline for the time being.
The ministry said housing starts had risen in the period leading up to the tax rise and the drop was a reaction to this.
The tax rise also did nothing to help improve Japan's labour market, where the unemployment rate is still hovering near record highs.

Japan announced on Friday that the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose to 3.3 percent in April, up from 3.2 percent in March and still within reach of the record high 3.5 percent marked last June.
A government official said weak housing starts had led to a decline in the number of construction workers.
"Although there are some signs of improvement, labour market conditions remain tough," the official said.
Most economists agree with the official view that the economy will eventually shake off the effects of the tax rise, but added that it will take some time before the fog clears.

"By the end of the summer, we may have a clear picture on the economy's outlook. But until then, we may get conflicting data and the financial markets may swing around," said Hisashi Yamada, an economist at the Japan Research Institute.
